events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Hellberg Safety investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current hearing-protection offering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.; Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, construction, or home improvement) with a new product or marketing approach.; 2) Expand the existing hearing-protection line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., fashion, lifestyle, or health) without a differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current hearing and face protection portfolio and existing B2B/industrial customers.; 4) Change the route to market or customer group (e.g., selling directly to consumers online, partnering with retailers, or targeting a new demographic) without altering the product.; 5) No expansion: maintain the current product mix and market focus, and not pursue new consumer propositions..

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a fashion or lifestyle accessory, because they are willing to pay a premium for stylish, comfortable earplugs that complement their personal style. Who benefits: Consumers seeking stylish, comfortable hearing protection; Hellberg Safety benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand differentiation.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as a fashion item, they will be motivated to own multiple pairs or styles, increasing purchase frequency and willingness to pay above the standard price point.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium price for design-led products, sell through fashion retailers, and build a lifestyle brand that differentiates it from generic industrial earplugs.. Assumptions: Consumers currently perceive hearing protection as utilitarian rather than fashion.; A design-led proposition can be produced at scale without compromising safety standards.; Fashion retailers are willing to stock and promote a differentiated consumer line.. Predictions: In a test offering a stylish, design-led earplug at a premium price, purchase intent among fashion-conscious consumers will be at least 20% higher than for a standard, functional earplug.; Surveyed consumers will rank style and comfort as top factors in choosing hearing protection, above price or safety requirements..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a safety requirement for specific high-risk activities (e.g., construction, rock concerts, or industrial work), because they will purchase it as a necessary protective item. Who benefits: Safety-conscious consumers in high-risk environments; Hellberg Safety benefits by selling purpose-specific, certified products and potentially securing contracts with employers.. Why behaviour changes: If hearing protection is framed as a mandatory safety item for a particular use case, consumers will act on the requirement rather than personal style or fashion, leading to higher purchase frequency.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price and market products as safety essentials, sell through industrial and safety retailers, and build a reputation for compliance and reliability in high-risk sectors.. Assumptions: There is a measurable demand for hearing protection in specific high-risk activities.; Safety regulations or employer requirements will continue to drive purchase decisions in these segments.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for certified, purpose-specific protection.. Predictions: In a test offering a purpose-specific earplug marketed as a safety requirement, purchase intent among workers and concert-goers will be at least 30% higher than for a generic, unbranded earplug.; Surveyed consumers will cite safety compliance or employer requirements as the primary reason for purchasing hearing protection..

Test "Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and purchase intent measurement.. Sample: 500 adults (age 18-45) recruited via an online panel, split equally between two groups: Fashion Group (n=250) and Safety Group (n=250).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) for a styled vs safety-specific earplug.. Predictions: T1: Fashion Group will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than Safety Group, and WTP will be higher for the styled earplug.; T2: Safety Group will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than Fashion Group, and WTP will be higher for the safety-specific earplug.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two groups is at least 20 percentage points and the Safety Group's purchase intent is at least 20% higher than the Fashion Group, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 20 points and the Fashion Group's purchase intent is at least 20% higher, conclude T1 is supported. If neither condition is met, the test is inconclusive and no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence does not demonstrate that consumers will pay a premium for stylish, fashion-led hearing protection, nor that safety requirements drive purchase decisions. A limited test (e.g., a 4-week survey with randomized messaging) is needed to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-A concerns a wear test on appearance and does not address consumer willingness to pay for stylish earplugs or whether fashion drives purchase decisions. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a fashion or lifestyle accessory, because they are willing to pay a premium for stylish, comfortable earplugs that complement their personal style.. Evidence: SYN-A.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence does not demonstrate that consumers will pay a premium for stylish, fashion-led hearing protection, nor that safety requirements drive purchase decisions. A limited test (e.g., a 4-week survey with randomized messaging) is needed to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent before committing resources. Target customer: Consumers seeking stylish, comfortable hearing protection for lifestyle or fashion purposes.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions Hellberg as a fashion brand, offering design-led, comfortable earplugs that complement personal style, with premium pricing and retail distribution.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test (500 adults, 4 weeks, €2,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for styled vs safety-specific earplugs.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to company assertions and a simulated wear test; no real consumer data shows willingness to pay for fashion-led hearing protection or that safety requirements drive purchase decisions.. Would change if: If the test shows a ≥20-point difference in purchase intent between the fashion and safety groups, and the safety group’s intent is at least 20% higher, T2 would become more likely and the recommendation would shift toward a safety-specific; If the test shows the fashion group’s purchase intent is at least 20% higher than the safety group, T1 would become more likely and the recommendation would shift toward a fashion-led proposition. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they view hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory that signals health awareness and safety commitment, leading them to purchase multiple pairs for different activities. Who benefits: Consumers seeking personal safety and style; Hellberg Safety benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty.. Why behaviour changes: Shifting perception from a medical necessity to a fashion and lifestyle item reduces price sensitivity and increases willingness to own multiple units.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium for design and brand differentiation, sell through retail or direct-to-consumer channels, and build a recurring revenue model with accessories.. Assumptions: Consumers currently perceive hearing protection as purely functional.; A lifestyle positioning can be effectively communicated to target demographics.; Retail or online channels can reach the intended consumer base.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate higher purchase intent for a lifestyle-branded hearing protection product compared to a purely functional product.; Willingness to pay will be higher for a differentiated proposition than for a standard industrial product.; Purchase intent will correlate with self-reported health-consciousness levels..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they need hearing protection for specific, high-frequency activities (e.g., construction, outdoor recreation) where standard earplugs are insufficient, creating a clear functional need that a differentiated product can address. Who benefits: Consumers with specific safety needs; Hellberg Safety benefits by offering a specialized product that meets those needs and can command higher margins.. Why behaviour changes: When a product directly solves a specific, high-frequency safety concern, consumers are more likely to purchase it than a generic hearing-protection item.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price the differentiated product at a premium, sell through specialized channels (e.g., construction suppliers, outdoor retailers), and offer accessories or upgrades for specific use cases.. Assumptions: There is a measurable segment of consumers who currently lack adequate protection for specific activities.; These consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that directly addresses their safety need.; Hellberg can differentiate its product with features tailored to those activities.. Predictions: Consumers will show higher purchase intent for a differentiated product marketed for specific activities compared to a generic product.; Willingness to pay will be higher for a product positioned as a solution to a specific safety concern.; Sales conversion will be higher in channels that target specific industries or activities..

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and choice-based conjoint design.. Sample: 500 adults recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and gender to reflect the target consumer base.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely). 2) Willingness to pay: 7-point Likert scale (1 = very low, 7 = very high). 3) Messaging preference: 3-point scale (lifestyle vs functional vs specific-use).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for a lifestyle-branded proposition than for a functional proposition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for a specific-use proposition than for a lifestyle proposition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the lifestyle proposition exceeds the functional proposition by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T1 is favoured. If the average purchase intent for the specific-use proposition exceeds the lifestyle proposition by at least 1.5 points, and the difference is statistically significant, then T2 is favoured. If neither difference reaches the threshold, the test is inconclusive and no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 2000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence does not demonstrate consumer demand for a lifestyle-branded hearing protection product, nor does it show a clear path to market or willingness to pay a premium. The market is not yet large enough to justify the investment. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

A differentiated consumer proposition would require additional market research to validate demand, willingness to pay,. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Conduct the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (or a similar survey) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for lifestyle-branded versus functional propositions before committing resources.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer hearing protection market in Europe and whether consumers perceive hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory are unknown. Evidence of demand is limited to company claims and does not establish consumer behavior.. Would change if: If the Consumer Proposition Preference Test shows a statistically significant difference in purchase intent between lifestyle and functional propositions, or if willingness to pay for a lifestyle proposition exceeds that for a functional; If new public sources reveal a growing consumer market for hearing protection or a clear willingness to pay premium for lifestyle-branded products.; If independent studies or market research demonstrate that consumers specifically need hearing protection for high-frequency activities and are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated product.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Home-Studio Buyer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product choices and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 200 respondents: 100 self-identified home-studio creators/podcasters and 100 individual buyers who have purchased studio equipment in the past year.. Measure: 1) Share of respondents choosing Neumann over a competitor (Brand A) for a simulated home-studio microphone. 2) Average WTP premium (EUR) that respondents would pay for Neumann over Brand A. 3) Percentage of respondents who cite "technical compatibility" as their top purchase reason.. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of creators will choose Neumann, and the average WTP premium will be below €50 (indicating price sensitivity).; T2: At least 60% of creators will choose Neumann, but the average WTP premium will be above €50, and more than 50% will cite "brand prestige" as their top reason.. Decision rule: If the observed share of creators choosing Neumann is at least 60% and the average WTP premium is below €50, proceed with a differentiated creator proposition (T1). If the share is at least 60% and the WTP premium is above €50, proceed with a prestige-driven proposition (T2). If neither condition is met, keep the single professional range.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Target customer: Home-studio owners and individual creators who need professional-grade audio for music, podcasting, or content creation.. Would change if: If the test shows less than 60% of creators choosing Neumann or average willingness-to-pay premium above €50, we would reconsider the differentiation strategy and focus on a single professional range.; If new evidence shows that brand prestige is the primary driver of purchase decisions, we would shift the value proposition toward prestige and limited-edition releases.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product because they value comfort, style, and lifestyle integration (e.g., fashion accessories or earbuds with built-in protection), leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking convenient, stylish ear protection for everyday use.. Why behaviour changes: Current hearing protection is often cumbersome, bulky, or utilitarian. A product that is designed as a fashion accessory or integrated into existing devices (e.g., AirPods) would reduce perceived effort and increase adoption.. How value is captured: Hellberg could charge a premium price for a design-led or smart product line sold through consumer channels, leveraging its existing brand and safety credibility.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that is perceived as stylish or integrated with popular devices.; The target segment (e.g., young adults, outdoor enthusiasts) has sufficient disposable income to purchase specialized ear protection.; Hellberg's design and safety reputation can be transferred to a consumer product without compromising performance.. Predictions: Surveyed target consumers would indicate higher purchase intent for a stylish earplug compared to a standard earplug.; Willingness to pay a premium price for a differentiated product would be at least 20% above the price of a standard earplug.; Sales conversion would be higher in online channels where product appearance is visible compared to B2B/industrial channels..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product because they need it for specific, high-risk activities (e.g., construction, industrial work, or loud events) where compliance and safety are mandatory, leading to repeat purchases and loyalty. Who benefits: Professional users and employers who must meet regulatory standards for hearing protection.. Why behaviour changes: Current hearing protection is often insufficient for high-risk environments, leading to non-compliance or injury. A product that meets or exceeds EN 352 standards and is designed for specific use cases would reduce legal and safety risks.. How value is captured: Hellberg could sell premium, compliance-certified products through B2B channels, leveraging its safety reputation and regulatory credibility.. Assumptions: Regulatory compliance is a primary purchase driver for industrial/professional users.; These users are willing to pay more for products that guarantee safety and meet standards.; Hellberg's existing B2B/industrial presence can be expanded into this segment without major retooling.. Predictions: Professional users would show higher purchase intent for a product that meets EN 352 standards compared to a standard earplug.; Willingness to pay would be at least 30% higher for a compliance-certified product than for a non-compliant one.; Repeat purchase rate would be higher for users who already purchase hearing protection for work..

Decision rule: If young adults' purchase intent exceeds industrial users' by at least 10 percentage points and their WTP premium is at least 20% higher, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting style/lifestyle. If industrial users' intent exceeds young adults' by at least 10 percentage points and their WTP premium is at least 20% higher, pursue a compliance/industrial proposition. If neither segment shows a significant advantage, do not expand.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406‑MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, demand, or market need for a consumer proposition.; Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., marine, aircraft, or other) and the technology’s suitability for it.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., marine survival beacon for individual boat owners).; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line to new commercial marine segments without a differentiated consumer proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine).; 4) Partner with or license the 406‑MHz technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than building a proprietary consumer product..

T1: Individual boat owners will adopt a consumer 406‑MHz distress beacon because they view it as a safety necessity for marine survival, and they would pay a premium for a reliable, legal device that meets federal standards. Who benefits: ACR Electronics and its B2B customers gain higher margins and expanded market reach by selling directly to consumers.. Why behaviour changes: If the device is marketed as a legal, effective marine survival tool, boat owners will shift from relying on traditional flares to a modern beacon, increasing purchase intent.. How value is captured: ACR would capture value through direct consumer sales, premium pricing, and potential licensing of the technology to marine equipment manufacturers.. Assumptions: Marine safety is a primary concern for individual boat owners in late 2002.; The 406‑MHz beacon is technically capable of reliable distress transmission.; Regulatory approval (FCC waiver) removes a significant barrier to consumer adoption.. Predictions: Surveyed boat owners will indicate intent to purchase a 406‑MHz beacon at a price above $50.; Sales of ACR’s existing B2B beacons will increase in regions where marine safety regulations are enforced.; Competitor beacons without 406‑MHz capability will show lower conversion rates among boat owners..

T2: Individual boat owners will adopt a consumer 406‑MHz distress beacon because they need a reliable, legal device for search and rescue, and they would pay a premium for a product that meets federal standards. Who benefits: ACR Electronics gains higher margins and expanded market reach by selling directly to consumers.. Why behaviour changes: If the device is marketed as a legal, effective search-and-rescue tool, boat owners will shift from relying on traditional flares to a modern beacon, increasing purchase intent.. How value is captured: ACR would capture value through direct consumer sales, premium pricing, and potential licensing of the technology to marine equipment manufacturers.. Assumptions: Search and rescue is a significant concern for individual boat owners in late 2002.; The 406‑MHz beacon is technically capable of reliable distress transmission.; Regulatory approval (FCC waiver) removes a significant barrier to consumer adoption.. Predictions: Surveyed boat owners will indicate intent to purchase a 406‑MHz beacon at a price above $50.; Sales of ACR’s existing B2B beacons will increase in regions where search-and-rescue regulations are enforced.; Competitor beacons without 406‑MHz capability will show lower conversion rates among boat owners..

Test "Marine Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.. Sample: 200 U.S. boat owners (self-identified) recruited via an online panel, stratified by boat ownership frequency.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willingness to pay (WTP).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of respondents will indicate purchase intent and WTP above $50, indicating marine safety as the primary driver.; T2: At least 30% of respondents will indicate purchase intent and WTP above $50, indicating search-and-rescue as the primary driver.. Decision rule: If purchase intent and WTP for the marine safety scenario meet or exceed the 30% threshold, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting marine safety. If the search-and-rescue scenario meets the threshold, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting search-and-rescue. If neither scenario meets the threshold, do not expand into a consumer proposition and continue focusing on B2B markets.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows the 406‑MHz beacon is legally available and already used in marine markets, but it does not prove individual boat owners purchase it for marine safety. Conduct the proposed Marine Safety Messaging Test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address whether individual boat owners purchase a 406‑ MHz beacon for marine safety. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: Individual boat owners will adopt a consumer 406‑ MHz distress beacon because they view it as a safety necessity for marine survival, and they would pay a premium for a reliable, legal device that meets federal standards.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows the 406‑ MHz beacon is legally available and already used in marine markets, but it does not prove individual boat owners purchase it for marine safety. Conduct the proposed Marine Safety Messaging Test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay before committing resources. Target customer: Individual boat owners in the United States who own boats and are concerned about marine safety.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions the 406‑ MHz beacon as a reliable, legal marine survival tool, offering a premium price for peace of mind and compliance with federal regulations.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Marine Safety Messaging Test (200 respondents, 10 weeks, €15,000) to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay for marine safety messaging.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the actual purchase behavior of individual boat owners remain uncertain. The test will provide data to resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent and willingness to pay below 30%, the investment case would weaken and we would reconsider expansion.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for search-and-rescue functionality, we would shift focus to T2.; If regulatory changes or market shifts make the consumer proposition unviable, we would abandon the expansion plan.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.; Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a safety product that meets regulatory standards (e.g., EN 352), because they trust certified safety labels and are willing to pay a premium for compliance. Who benefits: Hellberg Safety (through higher-margin consumer sales) and consumers (through certified, safe products).. Why behaviour changes: Consumers currently lack clear, accessible information about hearing protection standards. A differentiated proposition that highlights compliance and safety would reduce uncertainty and increase purchase intent.. How value is captured: Hellberg would capture value by selling certified, branded consumer products directly or through retailers, leveraging its existing R&D and manufacturing capabilities.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of hearing protection standards but struggle to find reliable information.; Regulatory compliance is a key purchase driver for safety-related products.; Hellberg can produce consumer-grade products that meet EN 352 standards at a cost-effective scale.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated consumer product with EN 352 certification, purchase intent or actual purchases will be higher than a baseline product without certification.; Surveyed consumers will cite safety certification as the primary reason for choosing the product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a lifestyle or fashion accessory, because they seek stylish, comfortable headwear that complements their personal style and daily activities. Who benefits: Hellberg Safety (through higher-margin lifestyle sales) and consumers (through fashionable, comfortable headwear).. Why behaviour changes: Consumers increasingly view headwear as an accessory rather than purely functional. A proposition that positions products as fashion items or lifestyle essentials would align with current consumer trends, increasing purchase intent.. How value is captured: Hellberg would capture value by branding and marketing consumer products as fashion items, potentially through dedicated lifestyle lines or collaborations, and by selling through fashion retailers.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for stylish, comfortable headwear.; Fashion and lifestyle are growing segments in the consumer safety market.; Hellberg can design and produce consumer-grade products that meet functional safety standards while maintaining aesthetic appeal.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated lifestyle product, purchase intent or actual purchases will be higher than a baseline product without lifestyle positioning.; Surveyed consumers will cite style and comfort as primary reasons for choosing the product..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Safety vs Lifestyle Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and purchase intent measurement.. Sample: 500 adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region (Europe). 250 participants see the safety-focused message; 250 see the lifestyle-focused message.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and stated reason for purchase (open-ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) for a product with EN 352 certification.. Predictions: T1: Participants shown the safety-focused message will have higher purchase intent and will cite safety certification as the primary reason, while those shown the lifestyle message will have lower intent.; T2: Participants shown the lifestyle-focused message will have higher purchase intent and will cite style and comfort as the primary reason, while those shown the safety message will have lower intent.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two message groups is statistically significant (p < 0.05) and the lifestyle group shows at least 10 percentage points higher intent than the safety group, proceed with a differentiated lifestyle proposition. If the safety group shows at least 10 percentage points higher intent, pursue a safety-focused proposition. If both groups show similar intent, no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence does not demonstrate consumer demand for a safety-focused proposition, nor does it quantify willingness to pay for compliance. A small-scale test (e.g., X1) is needed to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Individual boat owners will purchase a consumer-grade 406‑MHz beacon because they view it as a low‑cost, easy‑to‑use safety device, not as a military or B‑2b product. Who benefits: ACR Electronics gains direct consumer revenue and brand awareness.. Why behaviour changes: If the beacon is positioned as a portable, affordable safety item for boat owners, they will be motivated to purchase it for personal use rather than relying on existing emergency services or waiting for a crisis.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value through direct sales at a premium (e.g., $150‑$300) or through licensing the technology to marine retailers.. Assumptions: Boating owners are willing to pay a premium for a 406‑MHz beacon over standard ELTs.; Marketing can shift perception from military tool to consumer safety item.; Distribution channels (retail, online) exist for a consumer product.. Predictions: If offered a consumer proposition, at least 10% of targeted boat owners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Purchase intent will be higher for the 406‑MHz beacon compared to a generic ELT at a similar price point..

T2: Individual boat owners will purchase a consumer-grade 406‑ MHz beacon because they need a reliable, legal, and affordable way to signal distress in emergencies, especially when existing emergency services are unavailable or costly. Who benefits: ACR Electronics gains a new consumer revenue stream and brand visibility in marine safety.. Why behaviour changes: If the beacon is marketed as a compliant, low‑cost solution for personal safety, boat owners will act on the need to protect themselves and their crew, leading to purchase even without a crisis.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value through direct consumer sales, retail partnerships, or licensing the technology to marine equipment distributors.. Assumptions: Boating owners face uncertainty about emergency response capabilities and are willing to invest in a compliant safety device.; Regulatory compliance (e.g., Coast Guard requirements) creates a demand for a legal signal method.; The 406‑ MHz frequency is accepted as a viable consumer signal option.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer proposition, at least 15% of targeted boat owners will purchase within 12 weeks, even at a price point comparable to standard ELTs.; Purchase intent will be higher when the beacon is framed as a compliance‑required safety item rather than a luxury product..

Test "Consumer vs Compliance Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and purchase intent measurement.. Sample: 200 U.S. boat owners (100 per arm) recruited via marine forums and social media. Recruitment cost: ~$1,500.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) for a 406 MHz beacon.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP when messaging emphasizes low‑cost, easy‑to‑use safety device.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP when messaging emphasizes compliance with Coast Guard requirements and legal signal capability.. Decision rule: If purchase intent in the compliance arm exceeds the low‑cost arm by at least 10 percentage points, proceed with a consumer proposition focused on compliance. If the low‑cost arm exceeds the compliance arm by at least 10 percentage points, pursue a low‑cost consumer proposition. If both arms are within 5 percentage points of each other, do not expand.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a full consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows the 406 MHz beacon is already available and affordable for boats, but it does not demonstrate individual boat owners will purchase it. A low‑cost, easy‑to‑use positioning is more likely to generate demand than compliance messaging. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Compliance Messaging Test to resolve the uncertainty before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a full consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows the 406 MHz beacon is already available and affordable for boats, but it does not demonstrate individual boat owners will purchase it. A low cost, easy to use positioning is more likely to generate demand than compliance messaging. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Compliance Messaging Test to resolve the uncertainty before committing resources. Target customer: Individual boat owners (personal use) rather than commercial marine operators.. Value proposition: A portable, affordable 406 MHz beacon marketed as a low cost safety device for personal use, leveraging ACR’s existing technology and distribution channels.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer vs Compliance Messaging Test (200 U.S. boat owners, ~$1,500 recruitment, 10 week timeline) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under different messaging frames.. Uncertainty: Whether individual boat owners will purchase a consumer grade 406 MHz beacon, and whether the low cost positioning will outperform compliance messaging.. Would change if: If the Compliance Messaging Test shows purchase intent at least 10 percentage points higher than the Low Cost arm, we would shift focus to a compliance‑driven consumer proposition.; If both arms are within 5 percentage points of each other, we would not expand into a full consumer line.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: It is mid-1962. Should Deere & Company develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its tractor engineering? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, market demand, competitive landscape, and technical feasibility.; Evidence must address whether a differentiated proposition would create measurable demand or value capture.. T1: Homeowners will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they see the tractor as a specialized tool for a specific use case (e.g., small-scale landscaping, gardening), and they value the engineering reputation and reliability associated with John Deere. Who benefits: Homeowners who need a reliable, specialized lawn and garden tractor; Deere benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty.. Why behaviour changes: If homeowners perceive the tractor as a purpose-built solution rather than a generic farm machine, they will be willing to pay more for features and performance tailored to their needs.. How value is captured: Deere can sell through independent dealers with a differentiated product line, commanding higher price points than standard agricultural equipment.. Assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 have the disposable income to purchase a dedicated lawn and garden tractor.; Deere's engineering reputation is sufficient to differentiate the product from competitors.; Independent dealers can effectively promote and service a differentiated consumer proposition.. Predictions: In a test market, homeowners will express willingness to pay a premium price for a John Deere lawn and garden tractor compared to an equivalent competitor.; Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed as a specialized tool rather than a general farm tractor.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with higher homeowner density and interest in outdoor recreation..

T2: Homeowners will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they view the tractor as a status symbol and a status signal, indicating modernity and ownership of a premium outdoor space, leading them to seek a brand that reflects their lifestyle. Who benefits: Affluent homeowners who use outdoor spaces as a status display; Deere benefits by selling a premium, brand‑rich product that commands higher margins.. Why behaviour changes: If homeowners perceive the tractor as a status item, they will choose a brand that signals modernity and ownership of a well‑kept outdoor area, even if the functional need is limited.. How value is captured: Deere can price the product at a premium, sell through high‑margin independent dealers, and build brand loyalty that justifies higher prices.. Assumptions: Affluent homeowners in 1962 have discretionary income to purchase a status‑oriented lawn and garden tractor.; Brand perception of modernity and ownership is a significant purchase driver for this segment.; Independent dealers can effectively promote a brand‑rich consumer proposition.. Predictions: In a test market, homeowners will show higher purchase intent for a brand positioned as a status item compared to a functional, utilitarian proposition.; Willingness to pay will be higher for a product marketed as a lifestyle accessory rather than a tool.; Sales will be concentrated in affluent suburban and urban markets where status signaling is more prominent..

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 200 U.S. homeowners (ages 30-65) recruited via an online panel, stratified by region (suburban, urban) and household income.. Measure: 1) WTP to purchase a John Deere lawn and garden tractor priced at $1,200 (functional proposition). 2) WTP to purchase the same tractor priced at $1,500 (status proposition). 3) Intent to recommend the product to a friend.. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP for the $1,200 functional proposition than for the $1,500 status proposition, and higher purchase intent than for a competitor's product.; T2: Higher WTP for the $1,500 status proposition than for the $1,200 functional proposition, and higher purchase intent than for a competitor's product.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the functional proposition exceeds the WTP for the status proposition by at least $200 (e.g., $1,200 vs $1,500), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small-scale landscaping. If the status proposition's WTP exceeds the functional proposition's by at least $200, pursue a status‑oriented proposition. If both propositions are equally willing to pay, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small-scale landscaping and homeowner gardening, leveraging Deere's engineering reputation and existing dealer network. Begin with a limited pilot to test willingness to pay and demand before full-scale rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small-scale landscaping and homeowner gardening, leveraging Deere's engineering reputation and existing dealer network. Begin with a limited pilot to test willingness to pay and demand before full-scale rollout. Target customer: Homeowners (ages 30-65) in suburban and urban areas with small gardens who value reliability and are willing to pay a premium for a specialized tool.. Value proposition: A purpose-built John Deere lawn and garden tractor that combines Deere's engineering expertise with features tailored to small-scale landscaping, marketed through independent dealers to capture higher margins.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Proposition Preference Test (200 homeowners, $18,000, 10 weeks) to compare willingness to pay for functional vs. status propositions.. Uncertainty: Demand for a differentiated consumer proposition is uncertain; evidence shows Deere already produced 1,000 units in 1963, but no source confirms homeowner purchase intent or willingness to pay.. Would change if: If the test shows the status proposition's willingness to pay exceeds the functional proposition by at least $200, we would shift focus to a status‑oriented proposition.; If no test is conducted, we would maintain the status quo of no expansion and continue focusing on B2B/agricultural markets.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Hearing Protection" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 adults in Sweden and Germany, recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and gender to reflect target consumer demographics.. Measure: Average WTP in SEK for a differentiated hearing-protection product (e.g., a lifestyle or health-focused design) and intent to purchase multiple pairs.. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent for a lifestyle-framed product compared to a health-framed product.; T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent for a health-framed product compared to a lifestyle-framed product.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the lifestyle-framed product exceeds the health-framed product by at least 10% (e.g., SEK 150 vs SEK 140), proceed with a differentiated lifestyle proposition. If the difference is less than 10%, both propositions are considered and further testing is recommended.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle or fashion accessory, targeting young adults and outdoor enthusiasts. Use the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to validate demand before full product development. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Evidence: SYN-C.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle or fashion accessory, targeting young adults and outdoor enthusiasts. Use the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to validate demand before full product development. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, demand, or market need for a consumer proposition.; Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., marine, aircraft, or other) and the technology’s suitability for it.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., marine survival beacon for individual boat owners).; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line to new commercial marine segments without a differentiated consumer proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine).; 4) Partner with or license the 406‑MHz technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than building a proprietary consumer product..

T1: Individual boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts will adopt a consumer-oriented 406 MHz satellite distress beacon because they view it as a personal safety device for emergency situations at sea, and will be willing to pay a premium for a reliable, registered device. Who benefits: ACR Electronics (through higher-margin consumer sales) and individual boat owners and outdoor users who need emergency communication.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently lack reliable, low-cost emergency communication options; a consumer proposition reduces dependency on phone or radio, and the required RTCM certification and NOAA registration signal compliance, reducing perceivedC. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling registered 406 MHz devices directly to consumers, with premium pricing justified by compliance, RTCM certification, and the safety signal it provides.. Assumptions: There is sufficient market awareness of 406 MHz beacons among individual boat owners and outdoor users.; These consumers are willing to pay a price above the cost of a standard portable emergency light.; Regulatory compliance (NOAA registration and RTCM standards) does not deter purchase.; ACR can reach these consumers through existing distribution channels or new consumer-facing channels.. Predictions: In a test offering a registered 406 MHz beacon to individual boat owners, purchase intent or actual purchase rate will be at least 5% of targeted households.; Surveyed consumers will cite emergency situation protection as the primary reason for purchase.; Competing devices without RTCM certification will show lower purchase intent or no purchase at all..

T2: Individual boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts will adopt a consumer-oriented 406 MHz satellite distress beacon because they need reliable, low-cost emergency communication for marine and outdoor activities, and will be willing to pay a price that reflects the device's safety signal. Who benefits: ACR Electronics (through higher-margin consumer sales) and individual boat owners and outdoor users who need reliable emergency communication.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently lack reliable, low-cost emergency communication options; a consumer proposition provides a dedicated, registered device that meets RTCM standards, reducing dependency on phone or radio and offering a safety signal.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling registered 406 MHz devices directly to consumers, with premium pricing justified by the safety signal, RTCM certification, and the reduced risk of not receiving a distress signal.. Assumptions: There is a measurable demand for reliable emergency communication among individual boat owners and outdoor users.; These consumers are willing to pay a price above the cost of a standard portable emergency light.; Regulatory compliance (NOAA registration and RTCM standards) does not deter purchase.; ACR can reach these consumers through existing distribution channels or new consumer-facing channels.. Predictions: In a test offering a registered 406 MHz beacon to individual boat owners, purchase intent or actual purchase rate will be at least 5% of targeted households.; Surveyed consumers will cite reliability and safety as the primary reason for purchase.; Competing devices without RTCM certification will show lower purchase intent or no purchase at all..

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Emergency vs Reliability" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: Condition A emphasizes emergency protection and the safety signal (e.g., "Save lives at sea with a registered 406 MHz beacon that works when phone or radio fail."), Condition B emphasizes reliability and low cost (e.g., "Get a trusted, RTCM-certified beacon that delivers a distress signal when you need it most."). Both conditions include a price point and a "Buy" option. The test measures purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this beacon?") and stated reason for purchase.. Sample: 200 U.S. adults who own a boat or have been on a boat in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel. Randomly assigned 100 to Condition A and 100 to Condition B.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (binary) and stated reason for purchase (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will achieve a purchase intent rate of at least 5% and emergency protection will be the top stated reason.; T2: Condition B will achieve a purchase intent rate of at least 5% and reliability will be the top stated reason.. Decision rule: If Condition A achieves a purchase intent rate of at least 5% and emergency protection is the top stated reason, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual boat owners. If Condition B achieves a purchase intent rate of at least 5% and reliability is the top stated reason, pursue a reliability-focused consumer proposition. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer sales.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, but they do not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or ACR’s ability to reach individual boat owners. Conduct the proposed Consumer Messaging Test to measure purchase intent and stated reasons before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources confirm the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, but they do not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or ACR’s ability to reach individual boat owners. Conduct the proposed Consumer Messaging Test to measure purchase intent and stated reasons before committing resources. Target customer: Individual boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts who need reliable emergency communication at sea.. Value proposition: A registered 406 MHz satellite distress beacon that provides a safety signal when phone or radio fail, meeting RTCM certification and NOAA requirements.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Messaging Test (Condition A vs Condition B) to determine whether emergency protection or reliability drives purchase intent.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, willingness to pay a premium, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers remain uncertain. Public sources do not show actual purchase behavior or demand.. Would change if: If the Consumer Messaging Test shows a purchase intent rate below 5% or reliability is the top stated reason, we would reconsider a consumer proposition or explore other alternatives.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand or ACR already reaches individual buyers, we would reassess the investment case.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer vs Small-Farm Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Recruit 400 respondents: 200 self-identified homeowners (age 30-65) and 200 small-farm owners (age 40-65). Randomly assign half to see a homeowner-focused lawn tractor description (status, convenience, and premium pricing) and half to see a small-farm owner-focused description (labor cost savings, efficiency, and premium pricing). Measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 0-100 scale.. Sample: 400 respondents (200 homeowners, 200 small-farm owners) from the United States, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 0-100 scale.. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and WTP for the homeowner-focused description than small-farm owners.; T2: Small-farm owners will show higher purchase intent and WTP for the small-farm-focused description than homeowners.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the homeowner-focused group is at least 20 points higher than the small-farm group, proceed with a differentiated homeowner proposition. If the difference is less than 20 points, do not invest. If the small-farm group shows higher WTP, pursue a small-farm proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) for a differentiated Deere lawn tractor at three price points ($1,500, $1,800, $2,000). 2) Primary driver ranking (convenience vs safety vs other).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will rank convenience as the top driver and show a WTP of at least $1,800, with a purchase intent of at least 15% at the $2,000 price point.; T2: Homeowners will rank safety as the top driver and show a WTP of at least $1,800, with a purchase intent of at least 15% at the $2,000 price point.. Decision rule: If the WTP at the $2,000 price point exceeds $1,800 for both convenience and safety drivers, proceed with a differentiated proposition targeting both convenience and safety. If only one driver meets the threshold, focus on that driver. If neither meets the threshold, do not invest.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Test "Consumer vs Small-Farm Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Recruit 400 respondents: 200 self-identified homeowners (age 30-65) and 200 small‑farm owners (age 40-65). Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and WTP for the differentiated small‑scale proposition than small‑farm owners.; T2: Small‑farm owners will show higher purchase intent and WTP for the differentiated small‑farm proposition than homeowners.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two groups is at least 5 percentage points and the WTP difference is at least $200, proceed with the differentiated proposition for the respective group. Test "Style vs Compliance Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from two distinct segments: (1) safety-conscious professionals (construction, industrial, extreme outdoor) and (2) general consumers. Each segment sees one of two product descriptions: style-specific (e.g., fashion-forward design, multiple color options) or compliance-specific (e.g., meets EN 352 standards for high-risk use). Both segments also see a price point 15% above standard protection. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 400 participants: 200 safety-conscious professionals and 200 general consumers, balanced across gender and age. Randomly assigned to one of four message groups (style or compliance).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each message.. Predictions: T1: General consumers will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the style-specific message than for the compliance-specific message.; T2: Safety-conscious professionals will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the compliance-specific message than for the style-specific message.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the style-specific message in the general consumer group is at least 5 points higher than for the compliance-specific message, proceed with a differentiated style proposition. If the average purchase intent for the compliance-specific message in the safety-conscious group is at least 5 points higher than for the style-specific message, proceed with a compliance proposition. If neither difference meets the 5‑point threshold, do not expand.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

T1: Fitness enthusiasts will adopt a home body-fat analyser because they seek precise, repeatable measurements to track progress and stay motivated. Who benefits: Fitness enthusiasts who want to monitor body composition without visiting a clinic.. Why behaviour changes: They currently rely on manual methods or generic scales; a dedicated device offers accuracy and convenience, prompting them to purchase and use it regularly.. How value is captured: Tanita can charge a premium for a consumer-grade device, sell directly to consumers, and potentially license the technology to fitness brands.. Assumptions: Fitness enthusiasts are willing to pay for a dedicated body-fat analyser.; The device is accurate enough to be trusted by consumers.; Distribution channels exist to reach individual buyers.. Predictions: If offered a consumer proposition, a survey of fitness enthusiasts would show >30% intent to purchase within 12 months.; Sales of a consumer version would exceed $1 million in the first year if priced at $150-$200..

T2: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser because they want to reduce risk of chronic diseases such as heart disease and diabetes, and they trust medical evidence that links excess body fat to these conditions. Why behaviour changes: They currently rely on generic scales or manual methods; a device that provides measurable, repeatable body-fat data would increase their willingness to purchase and use it regularly.. How value is captured: Tanita can position the device as a health tool, price it at a premium, and sell directly to consumers, potentially leveraging its medical credibility to command higher margins.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of the health risks associated with excess body fat.; They trust medical evidence that body fat is a risk factor.; They are willing to pay for a device that provides measurable health insights.. Predictions: If offered a health-focused proposition, a survey of health-conscious consumers would show >30% intent to purchase within 12 months.; Sales of a health-focused version would exceed $1 million in the first year if priced at $150-$200..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Fitness Enthusiasts vs Health-Conscious Consumers" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a home body-fat analyser proposition. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Fitness Enthusiast Group (n=200) and Health-Conscious Group (n=200). Each group sees a product description of a stand-on body-fat analyser priced at $150-$200, with a call-to-action to purchase. The survey measures purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP).. Sample: 2,000 adults aged 18-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants indicating "Would buy") and average WTP (dollars) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Fitness Enthusiast Group will have a purchase intent rate of at least 30% and an average WTP of at least $180, while Health-Conscious Group will have a rate below 20% and WTP below $120.; T2: Health-Conscious Group will have a purchase intent rate of at least 30% and an average WTP of at least $180, while Fitness Enthusiast Group will have a rate below 20% and WTP below $120.. Decision rule: If the Fitness Enthusiast Group meets both thresholds (purchase intent ≥30% and WTP ≥$180), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting fitness enthusiasts. If the Health-Conscious Group meets both thresholds, proceed with a health-focused proposition. If neither group meets both thresholds, do not expand.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

A test is needed to measure actual purchase intent and willingness to pay before committing capital Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Lifestyle vs Compliance Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from two distinct segments: outdoor/recreational enthusiasts (n=200) and safety-conscious professionals/employers (n=200). Each segment views two product descriptions of a differentiated Hellberg line: one emphasizing lifestyle/design (e.g., "Stylish, comfortable earplugs for outdoor adventures"), and one emphasizing compliance with EN 352 standards (e.g., "Certified hearing protection for construction and industrial use"). After viewing both descriptions, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 400 participants (200 outdoor/recreational enthusiasts and 200 safety professionals/employers) from Europe, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR) for each messaging condition.. Predictions: T1: Outdoor/recreational segment will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the lifestyle message than for the compliance message.; T2: Safety professionals/employers will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the compliance message than for the lifestyle message.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the lifestyle message in the outdoor segment is at least 5 points higher than for the compliance message, proceed with a differentiated lifestyle proposition. If the average purchase intent for the compliance message in the safety segment is at least 5 points higher than for the lifestyle message, proceed with a differentiated compliance proposition. If neither difference meets the 5‑point threshold, do not expand.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Target customer: Outdoor/recreational enthusiasts and safety-conscious professionals/employers in Europe, as indicated by Hellberg’s existing consumer line and the need to test purchase intent.. Value proposition: A differentiated Hellberg line that combines innovative design, comfort, and safety certification (EN 352), positioned as a lifestyle accessory for outdoor activities and a compliant product for regulated environments.. Would change if: If the test shows a 5-point or greater difference in purchase intent between lifestyle and compliance messaging, the recommendation would shift to pursue a differentiated lifestyle proposition.; If additional evidence shows strong consumer demand for multiple purchases or premium pricing, the recommendation would be to invest in a differentiated line.; If no test result meets the 5-point threshold, the recommendation would remain to maintain the current product mix and market focus.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory that adds convenience and style, leading to multiple purchases. Why behaviour changes: Current hearing protection is often bulky and utilitarian. If marketed as a fashion item or accessory, consumers will be motivated to own multiple units.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through premium pricing, brand extension, and recurring revenue from accessories and consumables.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a differentiated product at a higher price point compared to standard hearing protection.; Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed as fashion or lifestyle than for a purely functional product.; Repeat purchase rate will be higher for a differentiated line than for a standard product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they face a specific, high-risk use case (e.g., construction, industrial, or extreme outdoor) where hearing protection is legally required or essential for safety, leading to compliance-driven purchases. Who benefits: Professional users and employers in regulated environments who need certified hearing protection.. Why behaviour changes: Current hearing protection is often generic and not sufficient for safety standards. A differentiated product that meets specific standards (e.g., EN 352) will be required for compliance, prompting purchases.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through premium pricing, B2B contracts, and compliance certification, leveraging its existing safety reputation.. Assumptions: Regulatory bodies will continue to enforce hearing protection standards in high-risk industries.; Professional users will prioritize certified protection over style.; Hellberg can obtain and market compliance certifications effectively.. Predictions: Purchase intent will be higher among professionals in regulated industries than among general consumers.; Contracts with employers will be signed at higher volumes than consumer sales.; Repeat purchase rate will be lower for a compliance-focused line than for a lifestyle line..

Test "Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: Condition A (lifestyle/fashion) or Condition B (compliance/professional). Both conditions present a product concept (Hellberg's differentiated consumer proposition) with identical features but framed differently.. Sample: 300 participants: 150 general consumers (recruited via an online panel) and 150 professionals/employers (recruited via industry forums and LinkedIn).. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Condition B, indicating a lifestyle-driven demand.; T2: Condition B will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Condition A, indicating a compliance-driven demand.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, proceed with a differentiated lifestyle proposition. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least 1.5 points, pursue a compliance-driven proposition. If the difference is below 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and focus on existing B2B/industrial customers.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Premium vs. Value Proposition Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two randomized conditions. Participants are shown a product description of a Jotun home protection coating (same product, same price point) and asked to indicate whether they would purchase it. Condition A sees a value‑focused message emphasizing price and availability. Condition B sees a premium‑focused message emphasizing brand trust and marine expertise. Both conditions include a willingness‑to‑pay question.. Sample: 400 Norwegian homeowners aged 25‑55, recruited via an online panel to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willing to pay (continuous).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition B, because the value proposition aligns with the existing direct‑to‑consumer channel.; T2: Condition B will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition A, because the premium‑focused message leverages brand trust and marine expertise.. Decision rule: If purchase intent in Condition A is at least 15 percentage points higher than in Condition B (p < 0.05), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on value. If purchase intent in Condition B is at least 15 percentage points higher than in Condition A, proceed with a premium‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is <5 percentage points, do not expand; if both conditions are equal, no expansion is justified.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

T1: Fitness enthusiasts will adopt a home body-fat analyser because they seek precise, repeatable measurements to track progress and stay motivated. Who benefits: Fitness enthusiasts who want data-driven insights into body composition.. Why behaviour changes: They currently rely on manual methods or generic scales; a dedicated device offers accuracy and convenience, prompting purchase.. How value is captured: Tanita can charge a premium for a differentiated consumer model, sell directly to consumers via retail or online channels, and potentially license the technology to fitness brands.. Assumptions: Fitness enthusiasts are willing to pay for a dedicated body-fat analyser.; The device will provide meaningful data that motivates them to track progress.; Retail distribution can reach individual buyers effectively.. Predictions: Surveyed fitness enthusiasts will indicate intent to purchase a home body-fat analyser at a price above $50.; Purchase intent will be higher among users who currently use manual methods or generic scales.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with high fitness participation rates..

T2: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser because they seek evidence-based insights to manage chronic conditions such as diabetes and heart disease. Why behaviour changes: They currently rely on general health advice or manual methods; a device that provides measurable, repeatable data will motivate them to act on health outcomes.. How value is captured: Tanita can position the device as a health management tool, sell through health retailers or online, and potentially offer subscription services for data analysis.. Assumptions: Consumers with chronic conditions are willing to pay for a health-focused body-fat analyser.; The device will provide data that they can use to make informed health decisions.; Regulatory approval for health claims can be obtained.. Predictions: Surveyed individuals with chronic conditions will indicate intent to purchase a home body-fat analyser at a price above $50.; Purchase intent will be higher among users who currently use manual methods or generic scales.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with high prevalence of chronic conditions..

Test "Purchase Intent Survey by Use Case" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 fitness enthusiasts (recruited via fitness forums and social media) and 250 adults with chronic conditions (recruited via health forums and clinics).. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (Would you buy a home body-fat analyser for a specific use case? Yes/No). 2) WTP: maximum price they would pay for the device (EUR). 3) Self-reported importance of body-fat measurement (1-5 scale).. Predictions: T1: Fitness enthusiasts will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP than adults with chronic conditions.; T2: Adults with chronic conditions will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP than fitness enthusiasts.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent among fitness enthusiasts is at least 15% higher than among adults with chronic conditions (p < 0.05), we conclude T1 is more likely. If the average WTP for fitness enthusiasts is at least 20% higher than for adults with chronic conditions (p < 0.05), we conclude T1 is more likely. If neither difference is statistically significant, we conclude neither theory is supported and no expansion is justified.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources from 1993 show Tanita already had a professional B2B body-fat analyser and a household bathroom scale, but no direct evidence of consumer demand. A proposed test (Purchase Intent Survey by Use Case) is needed to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for fitness enthusiasts versus adults with chronic conditions. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources from 1993 show Tanita already had a professional B2B body-fat analyser and a household bathroom scale, but no direct evidence of consumer demand. A proposed test (Purchase Intent Survey by Use Case) is needed to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for fitness enthusiasts versus adults with chronic conditions. Target customer: Fitness enthusiasts who seek precise, repeatable body-fat measurements to track progress.. Value proposition: A differentiated home body-fat analyser that provides accurate, repeatable measurements, leveraging Tanita’s existing B2B technology and brand credibility.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Purchase Intent Survey by Use Case (500 respondents, 10 weeks, €15,000) to test purchase intent and willingness to pay for fitness enthusiasts versus adults with chronic conditions.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to pre-1993 sources; no direct data on consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market fit exists. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the survey shows purchase intent among fitness enthusiasts is not significantly higher than among adults with chronic conditions, or if willingness to pay is not above a threshold (e.g., >$50), we would reconsider expansion.; If new evidence from 1993 shows strong consumer demand, we would revise the recommendation to proceed with a consumer proposition.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
Lawn and garden equipment sales rise 76 percent.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
