Test "Certified vs Styled Earplugs Consumer Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized product exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a styled, branded earplug marketed as EN 352 certified for outdoor recreation; Group B sees the same earplug marketed as a fashion accessory for leisure activities. Both groups see a generic unbranded earplug as a control. Participants report purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 300 adults aged 18–45 who have purchased hearing protection in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel. Randomly split into two equal groups (150 per group).. Measure: Purchase intent score (Group A vs Group B) and willingness to pay (EUR) for the certified styled earplug versus the generic unbranded earplug.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a purchase intent score at least 10 points higher than Group B, and willingness to pay will be at least EUR 5 higher than for the generic earplug.; T2: Group B will have a purchase intent score at least 10 points higher than Group A, and willingness to pay will be at least EUR 5 higher than for the generic earplug.. Decision rule: If Group A’s purchase intent score is at least 10 points higher than Group B and its willingness to pay is at least EUR 5 higher than for the generic earplug, proceed with a differentiated certified consumer proposition. If Group B’s score is higher, pursue a fashion‑focused proposition. If neither difference is statistically significant, do not expand.. Cost: 3000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows Hellberg already sells hearing protection to individual buyers and has a consumer line for children, but no source shows consumers actively seek or pay a premium for EN 352 certification. A small, low-cost test is needed to measure willingness to pay for a certified styled earplug versus a generic one. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows Hellberg already sells hearing protection to individual buyers and has a consumer line for children, but no source shows consumers actively seek or pay a premium for EN 352 certification. A small, low-cost test is needed to measure willingness to pay for a certified styled earplug versus a generic one. Target customer: Individual consumers who purchase hearing protection for recreational activities, leisure, or home improvement, particularly those who already use generic earplugs.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that clearly communicates EN 352 certification, offering a premium-priced, stylish earplug for outdoor recreation and leisure activities.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Certified vs Styled Earplugs Consumer Test (300 adults, 6 weeks, €3,000) to measure willingness to pay for a certified styled earplug versus a generic one.. Uncertainty: The size of the premium willingness to pay for certified products is unknown; evidence does not show consumers actively seek or pay for certification, nor that they are price-sensitive to certified products.. Would change if: If the test shows a willingness to pay premium of at least €5 for the certified styled earplug and a purchase intent difference of at least 10 points between the certified and generic groups, proceed with a differentiated certified consumer; If the test shows no significant difference in purchase intent or willingness to pay between the certified and generic groups, do not expand. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

Both see a price point and a willingness-to-pay question.. Sample: 300 participants: 150 home-studio creators and 150 individual buyers, recruited via social media and audio forums.. Predictions: T1: Participants shown technical messaging will report higher WTP and higher importance of technical performance than those shown aesthetic messaging.; T2: Participants shown aesthetic messaging will report higher WTP and higher importance of aesthetic design than those shown technical messaging.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the technical group exceeds the average WTP for the aesthetic group by at least 10% points (e.g., €120 vs €110), proceed with a differentiated technical proposition. If the difference is less than 5% points, keep the single professional range. If the difference is 5% points or more, the aesthetic theory is more likely and we would. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Who benefits: Consumers seeking comfortable, stylish earplugs for recreational activities and fashion-conscious individuals.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is framed as a fashion item, consumers shift from utilitarian use to multiple purchases for different settings, increasing repeat purchases.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through premium pricing, design-led product lines, and direct-to-consumer or retail partnerships that emphasize aesthetics.. Assumptions: Consumers currently view hearing protection as purely functional.; Fashion and lifestyle influence purchase decisions for earplugs.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for stylish, comfortable earplugs.. Predictions: In a test offering a stylish, comfortable earplug at a premium price, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard industrial earplug.; Consumers will report higher willingness to purchase multiple pairs for different activities.; Sales will be driven by fashion and lifestyle messaging rather than purely functional positioning..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a health necessity, because they are willing to pay for proven protection against noise-induced hearing loss. Who benefits: Health-conscious consumers, parents of children, and individuals at high risk of hearing damage.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is framed as a medical necessity, consumers shift from utilitarian use to consistent use across activities, reducing the need for multiple products.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through premium positioning, health messaging, and partnerships with healthcare providers or insurance companies that emphasize protection.. Assumptions: Consumers currently view hearing protection as optional.; Health concerns drive purchase decisions for earplugs.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for products marketed as medical necessity.. Predictions: In a test offering a health-focused earplug at a premium price, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard industrial earplug.; Consumers will report higher intent to use the product consistently across activities.; Sales will be driven by health messaging rather than fashion or lifestyle positioning..

Test "Fashion vs Health Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults interested in hearing protection. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions for a new, stylish, comfortable earplug (Fashion Condition) or one for the same earplug marketed as a health necessity (Health Condition). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) to ensure statistical power.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Fashion Condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Health Condition.; T2: Health Condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Fashion Condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the Fashion Condition is at least 5 points higher than the Health Condition, adopt the fashion proposition. If the difference is less than 5 points, adopt the health proposition. If the difference is less than 2 points, no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a stylish, comfortable accessory for recreational and fashion-conscious users. Use premium pricing and design-led marketing to capture value. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a stylish, comfortable accessory for recreational and fashion-conscious users. Use premium pricing and design-led marketing to capture value. Target customer: Fashion-conscious adults and recreational users who currently view hearing protection as purely functional.. Value proposition: A stylish, comfortable earplug that combines safety with aesthetic appeal, offering multiple pairs for different activities and a premium price reflecting design and quality.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Fashion vs Health Messaging Test (300 participants, 4 weeks, €2,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under each condition.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to company claims and a single independent study; no source reads directly address consumer willingness to pay for a differentiated proposition.. Would change if: If the test shows the Health Condition achieving at least a 5-point higher purchase intent than the Fashion Condition, the recommendation would shift to a health-focused proposition.; If no test is conducted, the recommendation would remain based on the assumption that fashion drives adoption, but the evidence is insufficient to confirm this.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Hellberg Safety investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current hearing-protection offering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.; Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, construction, or home improvement) with a new product or marketing approach.; 2) Expand the existing hearing-protection line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., fashion, lifestyle, or health) without a differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current hearing and face protection portfolio and existing B2B/industrial customers.; 4) Change the route to market or customer group (e.g., selling directly to consumers online, partnering with retailers, or targeting a new demographic) without altering the product.; 5) No expansion: maintain the current product mix and market focus, and not pursue new consumer propositions..

Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, demand, or market need for a consumer proposition.; Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., marine, aircraft, or other) and the technology’s suitability for it.. T1: Individual boat owners will adopt a consumer emergency beacon because they fear lost or stranded marine survival and face increasing liability costs for non-compliance. Who benefits: ACR Electronics and related 406 MHz EPIRB/EPIRB+ suppliers, as the market grows beyond the military and B2B segments.. Why behaviour changes: If boat owners perceive a significant financial or legal penalty for not being equipped and the beacon provides a low-cost, required compliance solution, they will purchase it even if they already own other safety gear.. How value is captured: ACR can charge a premium over generic beacons and retain ownership of the brand and technology, while compliance regulators reduce penalty options.. Assumptions: Liability/penalties are a real deterrent in at least some marine insurance or registration regions.; The 406 MHz EPIRB is the only affordable, effective, legally required beacon for boats.; Boats can be serviced by marine dealers who already carry beacon inventory.. Predictions: If a test shows a high willingness to pay a premium (e.g., $150 vs $70 for a generic beacon) among surveyed marine owners, the theory is supported.; If a survey shows a majority of boat owners would purchase a beacon even if they already own other safety equipment, the theory is supported.; If a pilot shows purchase conversion among those who have already purchased marine safety gear, the theory is supported..

T2: Individual boat owners will adopt a consumer emergency beacon because they want to be seen as responsible, safe, and to avoid insurance or registration penalties, and they already buy marine safety gear. Who benefits: ACR Electronics and related 406 MHz EPIRB/EPIRB+ suppliers, as the market grows beyond the military and B2B segments.. Why behaviour changes: If boat owners perceive being equipped as a sign of care and compliance, they will purchase a beacon even if they already own other safety equipment, because they want to avoid penalties and be seen as responsible.. How value is captured: ACR can charge a premium over generic beacons and retain ownership of the brand and technology, while compliance regulators reduce penalty options.. Assumptions: Insurance or registration penalties for not being equipped are a real deterrent in at least some marine regions.; The beacon is the only affordable, effective, legally required device for boats.; Boats can be serviced by marine dealers who already carry beacon inventory.. Predictions: If a test shows a high willingness to pay a premium among boat owners who already own marine safety gear, the theory is supported.; If a survey shows a majority of boat owners would purchase a beacon even if they already own other safety equipment, the theory is supported.; If a pilot shows purchase conversion among those who already own marine safety gear, the theory is supported..

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Marine Owners" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 200 U.S. marine boat owners (owning 1-5 years, 50k+ value) recruited via marine forums and boat clubs.. Measure: Average WTP for a 406 MHz EPIRB (premium vs generic beacon) and self-reported importance of liability/penalties vs being seen as responsible.. Predictions: T1: WTP premium > $70; self-reported liability/penalties as primary motivator.; T2: WTP premium < $70; self-reported being seen as responsible as primary motivator.. Decision rule: If average WTP premium exceeds $80 (premium vs generic) AND at least 60% of respondents cite liability/penalties as primary motivator, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition. If WTP premium is below $70 AND at least 60% cite being seen as responsible, pursue a different route. If neither threshold is met, do not expand.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Target customer: Individual marine boat owners (owning 1-5 years, $50k+ value) in U.S. marine regions where liability/penalties are a deterrent.. T1: Consumers will adopt a stand-on body-fat analyser for home use if they view it as a health monitoring tool, because they already keep track of body composition and seek evidence of excess fat. Who benefits: Fitness enthusiasts and health-conscious individuals who currently rely on manual methods or professional measurements.. Why behaviour changes: They would switch from self-tracking (e.g., tape measure, food diary) to a device that provides a measurable, repeatable result, reducing uncertainty about weight changes.. How value is captured: Tanita would sell a premium-priced home unit directly to consumers, capturing margin through direct sales and brand positioning as a health tool.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of body-fat health risks (heart disease, diabetes) and are motivated to measure them.; Home use is feasible without requiring a technician or specialized setting.; Price sensitivity is low enough that a differentiated home unit can be sold at a premium.. Predictions: In a test offering a stand-on analyser to fitness enthusiasts, purchase intent or actual purchase will be higher than for a standard digital scale.; Surveyed respondents will cite health monitoring as the primary reason for choosing the device.; Sales will be concentrated in regions where health awareness is high (e.g., Japan, parts of Europe)..

T2: Consumers will adopt a stand-on body-fat analyser for home use if they view it as a convenient, non-invasive alternative to professional measurements, because they value speed and ease of use. Who benefits: Busy individuals who prefer quick, at-home health checks over clinic visits or manual methods.. Why behaviour changes: They would switch from scheduling appointments or using tape measures to a device that provides an immediate, repeatable result, reducing time and effort.. How value is captured: Tanita would sell a low-cost, easy-to-use home unit through retail or direct channels, capturing volume sales and brand as a time-saving health tool.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience and speed over accuracy in health monitoring.; Home use is feasible without requiring technical expertise or specialized settings.; Price sensitivity is moderate, allowing a mid-priced home unit to be competitive.. Predictions: In a test offering a stand-on analyser to busy professionals, purchase intent or actual purchase will be higher than for a standard digital scale.; Surveyed respondents will cite convenience as the primary reason for choosing the device.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with high disposable income and time constraints (e.g., parts of North America)..

Test "Purchase Intent Test: Health Monitoring vs Convenience" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a health-focused stand-on analyser described as a tool for tracking body composition and excess fat, emphasizing medical evidence and accuracy. Group B sees the same device described as a convenient, quick health check requiring no technical skill or appointment. Both groups see a standard digital scale as a baseline. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 adults (150 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region (Japan, US, Europe).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10 scale) and maximum price willingness to pay for the stand-on analyser.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Group B, because health monitoring is the primary driver.; T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Group A, because convenience is the primary driver.. Decision rule: If the mean purchase intent for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s mean ≥ 5.5) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), we conclude T1 is supported and recommend developing a health‑focused consumer proposition. If Group B’s mean is at least 5 points higher, we conclude T2 is supported and recommend a convenience‑focused proposition. If neither difference is significant, we conclude neither theory is well‑supported and recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources from 1993 show Tanita already had a professional B2B body-fat analyser and a household bathroom scale, but no direct evidence of consumer demand for a stand-on analyser. The purchase intent test (proposed) would be needed to decide, but the evidence base is weak. Continue monitoring the market and consider a pilot before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406‑MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, demand, or market need for a consumer proposition.; Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., marine, aircraft, or other) and the technology’s suitability for it.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., marine survival beacon for individual boat owners).; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line to new commercial marine segments without a differentiated consumer proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine).; 4) Partner with or license the 406‑MHz technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than building a proprietary consumer product..

T1: Individual boat owners will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they view the 406 MHz satellite beacon as a life-saving necessity for remote survival, and they are willing to pay a premium for a device that can be activated manually or automatically in an emergency. Who benefits: ACR Electronics and its B2B customers gain higher-margin consumer sales and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: If the beacon is marketed as a reliable, manual activation device for remote survival, boat owners will shift from relying on phone calls or radio to a self-contained signal that can be activated even without cell service.. How value is captured: ACR captures value through direct consumer sales, premium pricing, and brand extension beyond its existing B2B market.. Assumptions: Boat owners in remote areas face high emergency risks where traditional communication fails.; They are willing to invest in a device that can be activated manually or automatically.; The 406 MHz technology is technically suitable for consumer use.. Predictions: In a test offering a manual activation beacon to a sample of individual boat owners, purchase intent will be higher than for an automatic activation beacon.; Willingness to pay will be above the cost of a standard 406 MHz beacon, indicating a premium..

T2: Individual boat owners will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they view the 406 MHz satellite beacon as a reliable, automatic emergency signal that eliminates the need for manual activation, and they are willing to pay a premium for peace of mind in remote areas. Who benefits: ACR Electronics gains higher-margin consumer sales and brand extension beyond its B2B market.. Why behaviour changes: If the beacon is marketed as an automatic, self-activating device that can be triggered by a fall or immersion, boat owners will shift from relying on manual activation to a device that works even without their intervention.. How value is captured: ACR captures value through direct consumer sales, premium pricing, and brand extension into the individual market.. Assumptions: Automatic activation reduces the perceived risk of not being able to signal in an emergency.; Boat owners in remote areas are willing to pay more for a device that eliminates manual activation.; The 406 MHz technology can be adapted for automatic activation without compromising performance.. Predictions: In a test offering an automatic activation beacon to a sample of individual boat owners, purchase intent will be higher than for a manual activation beacon.; Willingness to pay will be above the cost of a standard 406 MHz beacon, indicating a premium for automatic functionality..

Test "Premium vs. Non-Premium Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from individual buyers who have purchased Neumann products in the past. They are shown two identical product pages for a new Neumann microphone, one with premium messaging emphasizing brand prestige and compatibility with existing professional equipment, and one with non-premium messaging emphasizing quality and performance. Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay and whether they would purchase.. Sample: 300 individual buyers who have purchased Neumann products in the past, randomly assigned to two groups of 150 each.. Measure: Maximum price willingness-to-pay (WTP) and purchase intent (binary: would buy).. Predictions: T1: Group with premium messaging will show higher WTP and higher purchase intent than group with non-premium messaging.; T2: Group with non-premium messaging will show higher WTP and higher purchase intent than group with premium messaging.. Decision rule: If premium messaging group WTP is at least 20% higher than non-premium messaging group WTP, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), then T1 is supported and a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators is recommended. If non-premium messaging group WTP is at least 20% higher, then T2 is supported and a differentiated proposition for individual buyers is recommended. If neither difference is statistically significant, the status quo of a single professional range for all customers remains appropriate.. Cost: 5000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers, emphasizing brand prestige and compatibility with existing professional equipment. This aligns with evidence of a growing home-studio market and positive response to the Home Studio Academy. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns packing errors and does not address consumer purchasing behavior, brand prestige, or willingness to pay for a differentiated proposition. Recommendation: Develop a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers, emphasizing brand prestige and compatibility with existing professional equipment. events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406‑MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, demand, or market need for a consumer proposition.; Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., marine, aircraft, or other) and the technology’s suitability for it.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., marine survival beacon for individual boat owners).; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line to new commercial marine segments without a differentiated consumer proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine).; 4) Partner with or license the 406‑MHz technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than building a proprietary consumer product..

T1: Individual boat owners and marine enthusiasts will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz distress beacon because they view it as a safety necessity for survival in remote marine emergencies. Who benefits: ACR Electronics gains premium pricing and recurring revenue through sales and rental of consumer units.. Why behaviour changes: Marine incidents are rare but life-threatening; users will purchase a beacon as a protective investment rather than as a luxury item.. How value is captured: Direct consumer sales and rental revenue, leveraging existing distribution channels to reach individual buyers.. Assumptions: Marine incidents are infrequent enough that the beacon is not perceived as a daily necessity.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a certified, reliable distress signal.; ACR can market the beacon as a safety product rather than a high-cost, complex device.. Predictions: Surveyed boat owners will indicate intent to purchase a consumer beacon at a price above $150.; Purchase intent will be higher for rental than for outright purchase.; Sales conversion will be driven by safety awareness campaigns rather than mass media..

T2: Individual boat owners and marine enthusiasts will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz distress beacon because they view it as a fashion accessory and status symbol, not a safety necessity. Who benefits: ACR Electronics gains premium pricing and brand equity through a lifestyle product line.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers increasingly treat safety gear as personal style; owning a visible, branded beacon signals membership in a community and adventure culture.. How value is captured: Premium-priced direct-to-consumer sales and limited-edition collaborations, leveraging existing retail channels.. Assumptions: Marine incidents are infrequent enough that the beacon is not perceived as a daily necessity.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a visible, branded device.; ACR can position the beacon as a lifestyle item rather than a technical survival tool.. Predictions: Surveyed marine enthusiasts will indicate intent to purchase a consumer beacon at a price above $200.; Purchase intent will be higher for limited-edition or branded variants than for generic models.; Sales will be driven by social media and community engagement rather than safety awareness..

Test "Consumer Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.. Sample: 200 marine enthusiasts and boat owners (100 per segment) recruited via marine forums and social media.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willing to pay (continuous).. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of marine enthusiasts will indicate purchase intent for a consumer beacon priced above $150, and rental intent will be higher than outright purchase.; T2: At least 60% of marine enthusiasts will indicate purchase intent for a consumer beacon priced above $200, and limited-edition variants will be preferred over generic models.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for the $150+ beacon (T1) is at least 60% among marine enthusiasts, proceed to develop a consumer proposition. If purchase intent for the $200+ beacon (T2) is at least 60%, develop a premium lifestyle line. If neither threshold is met, do not expand.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, not for fashion or status. Evidence of consumer demand is lacking; a test is needed to measure purchase intent. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, not for fashion or status. Evidence of consumer demand is lacking; a test is needed to measure purchase intent. Target customer: Individual boat owners and marine enthusiasts who need reliable distress signaling in remote marine environments.. Value proposition: A consumer-grade 406 MHz distress beacon that meets regulatory requirements for general public use, offering a certified, reliable way to alert search and rescue in remote marine emergencies.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (200 marine enthusiasts, $18,000, 10 weeks) to validate demand before committing to product development.. Uncertainty: Whether marine incidents are infrequent enough to make the beacon a safety purchase rather than a luxury item, and whether consumers will pay a premium for a certified device.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for a $150+ beacon among marine enthusiasts is below 60% (T1 is rejected).; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for a fashion or status beacon (T2 becomes more likely).. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.
